architectural_implications.after: Memory lives in the enterprise database alongside records, inheriting row/column entitlements and policy for retrieval and vector search.
architectural_implications.before: Agent memory lives in a separate vector database, with access control enforced in application code or prompts.
architectural_implications.consequence: Fewer leakage paths and one governance model, but the memory layer must now be schema-managed and migrated like primary data rather than treated as an ephemeral cache.
architectural_implications.observation: Memory is currently often implemented as an application-side vector store outside enterprise governance.

architectural_implications.after: A control plane owns identity, tool permissions, spend limits, and audit; an intelligence plane owns ontology, memory, semantic layer, and the learning loop.
architectural_implications.before: Orchestration code handles tool permissions, identity, memory, retrieval, and learning heuristics together.
architectural_implications.consequence: Clearer ownership and testability per plane; requires defining the interface where a knowledge request must still pass control-plane authorization.
architectural_implications.observation: Control and intelligence concerns are typically tangled in a single orchestration layer.

architectural_implications.after: Memory traces and corrections emitted by the harness become the training set for routing and decision models.
architectural_implications.before: Improvement requires assembling labeled datasets separately from the running system.
architectural_implications.consequence: Faster improvement loops, but memory retention policy, PII handling, and label quality become upstream dependencies of model training.
architectural_implications.observation: Fine-tuning data is usually sourced from curated datasets rather than production telemetry.

architectural_implications.after: Private AI services containers host models on-prem or in-cloud within organizational boundaries.
architectural_implications.before: LLMs, embeddings, and rerankers are called from external providers across organizational data boundaries.
architectural_implications.consequence: Stronger compliance and data-residency guarantees, at the cost of owning capacity planning, upgrades, and serving reliability.
architectural_implications.observation: Inference and embedding/reranker serving are usually outsourced to third-party APIs.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Richmond Alake
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: Agent architecture, memory, control planes, and intelligence planes using Oracle AI Database
  • Purpose: Educate AI engineers on moving beyond basic prompting and control planes toward the intelligence plane (knowledge, memory, and learning) to build superior, secure, and production-ready AI agents. Richmond Alake discusses how as foundational AI models commoditize and everyone has access to the same LLMs, differentiation in AI agents comes down to architecture: specifically the introduction of the Intelligence Plane alongside the Control Plane and Data Plane. He explores agent memory taxonomy, continuous learning, deep data security, and how Oracle AI Database tools enable building production-grade agents.

Topic Map

Agent Memory Taxonomy

  • Explanation: Defining agent memory across short-term (working memory, semantic cache) and long-term (semantic, episodic, procedural) structures, governed by the four R's: retain, reuse, recall, and refine.
  • Key claims:
    • Agent memory is how an agent retains, reuses, refines, and recalls what it learns across turns, sessions, and agents.
    • Memory management is critical for structuring agent workflows and reducing token costs.
  • Examples:
    • Short-term working memory vs long-term episodic or procedural memory.
  • Terminology:
    • agent memory
    • working memory
    • semantic cache
    • episodic memory
    • procedural memory
    • four R's
  • Why it matters: Without structured memory, agents cannot retain context or improve across user sessions.

Control Plane vs Intelligence Plane

  • Explanation: Differentiating between the control plane (governance, identity, tool permissions, and guardrails) and the intelligence plane (knowledge, memory, and continuous learning).
  • Key claims:
    • The control plane governs what an agent may do: who it is, what it may call, spending limits, and auditing.
    • Information does not equal intelligence; having the same models and data does not grant competitive advantage without the intelligence plane.
    • The intelligence plane decides what an agent knows, what it remembers, what it is allowed to see, and how it gets better over time.
  • Examples:
    • The historical parallel of Washington OP-20-G (control) vs Pearl Harbor Station HYPO (intelligence) decoding 'AF' as Midway during WWII.
  • Terminology:
    • control plane
    • intelligence plane
    • identity and access
    • policy and guardrails
    • continuous learning
  • Why it matters: Engineers need to build beyond orchestration and control to incorporate knowledge, memory, and learning into agent architectures.

Software Factory and Agent Workflows

  • Explanation: Applying Bob Bemer's 1968 software factory concept to AI agent production lines where specialized agents handle planning, building, and testing under human review gates.
  • Key claims:
    • A software factory is a production line where AI agents build software with specific tools, memory, and checks.
    • Humans decide the work and sign off on what ships to production.
  • Examples:
    • Plan agent, build agent, and test agent working in parallel with review gates.
  • Terminology:
    • software factory
    • production line
    • review gate
    • work queue
  • Why it matters: Enables reliable, repeatable software generation by chaining specialized agent roles.

Oracle AI Database & Deep Data Security

  • Explanation: Leveraging Oracle AI Database features for deep data security, private inference containers, ontology, semantic layers, and continual learning.
  • Key claims:
    • Oracle Deep Data Security propagates user permissions and row/column security policies into agent memory and vector searches.
    • Private AI Services Containers allow hosting LLMs, embeddings, and rerankers securely on-prem or in-cloud within organizational data boundaries.
  • Examples:
    • Governed analyst vs naive analyst querying financial data with and without ontology and semantic layers.
  • Terminology:
    • Oracle AI Database
    • deep data security
    • private AI services container
    • ontology
    • semantic layer
    • tokenomics
  • Why it matters: Ensures enterprise-grade security, compliance, and accurate data interpretation for mission-critical workflows.

Key Points

Agent = Model + Harness

  • Explanation: The model provides core intelligence, while the harness (tools, memory, checks) turns it into an operational agent.
  • Evidence: Equation presented in speaker slides outlining agent architecture components.
  • Practical implication: Engineers must focus heavily on building robust harnesses around foundation models.

Information != Intelligence

  • Explanation: Having access to the same data and models does not mean agents arrive at correct, secure, and optimal conclusions without structured intelligence layers.
  • Evidence: Historical WWII Station HYPO vs Washington example and financial analyst demo showing 97% vs 33% accuracy.
  • Practical implication: Invest in ontologies, semantic layers, and memory engineering rather than relying solely on base LLM capabilities.

Memory Traces as Training Data

  • Explanation: Capturing agent memory traces, corrections, and feedback provides the exact fine-tuning data needed to improve models over time.
  • Evidence: Demonstration of fine-tuning routing and decision models using recorded conversation memory and classifications.
  • Practical implication: Teams should log and convert agent memory and interactions into fine-tuning datasets.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

The Agent Stack & Intelligence Plane

  • How it works: Layers application, gateway, orchestration, reasoning, memory managers, tooling, security, memory core, and infrastructure, intersected by control and intelligence planes.
  • Components:
    • Control Plane
    • Intelligence Plane
    • Memory Core
    • Semantic Layer
    • Ontology
    • Continual Learning Loop
  • When to use: When designing enterprise agent architectures requiring governance, memory, and continuous improvement.

Examples & Case Studies

Comparing a governed financial analyst agent (using ontology and semantic layers) with a naive agent on complex financial queries.

  • Illustrates: The practical impact of the intelligence plane on accuracy, token cost, and tokenomics.
  • Lesson: Ontology and semantic layers drastically reduce token consumption and eliminate costly errors in mission-critical applications.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Treat memory as data and store it alongside enterprise records under proper governance.
    • Write down entities and definitions to model ontologies before letting agents query them.
    • Push entitlements and row-level security into the data layer so agents inherit permissions.
  • Strategic:
    • Shift architectural focus from simple prompt engineering to intelligence plane design.
    • Build or adopt systems that allow continual learning from memory traces to model weights.
    • Own your memory and inference infrastructure to maintain security and compliance.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How are your agent memory traces being captured and utilized for fine-tuning?
    • Are your semantic layers and ontologies robust enough to prevent hallucinations in mission-critical queries?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Bob Bemer coined the term software factory at GE in 1968. (historical)
  • Oracle AI Database provides deep data security propagating user row and column permissions into vector memory searches. (product capability)

Notable Quotes

"Agent memory is how an agent retains, reuses, refines and recalls what it learns, across turns, sessions and agents." (at 0:57) "Information does not equal intelligence." (at 15:30)

Compressed Summary

  • Foundational models are commodities; agent differentiation requires advanced architecture.
  • The intelligence plane governs what an agent knows, remembers, sees, and learns over time.
  • Oracle AI Database provides robust tooling for memory management, ontology, semantic layers, and deep data security.
  • Memory traces serve as training data for continual learning and fine-tuning decision models.
  • Keywords: agent memory, intelligence plane, control plane, ontology, oracle ai database, continual learning
  • Core insight: As AI models commoditize, true agent differentiation and reliability come from building a robust intelligence plane encompassing managed memory, ontologies, semantic layers, and continual learning.

### Agent = Model + Harness
- **Explanation**: The model provides core intelligence, while the harness (tools, memory, checks) turns it into an operational agent.

- **Practical implication**: Engineers must focus heavily on building robust harnesses around foundation models.
### Information != Intelligence
- **Explanation**: Having access to the same data and models does not mean agents arrive at correct, secure, and optimal conclusions without structured intelligence layers.
- **Evidence**: Historical WWII Station HYPO vs Washington example and financial analyst demo showing 97% vs 33% accuracy.
- **Practical implication**: Invest in ontologies, semantic layers, and memory engineering rather than relying solely on base LLM capabilities.

- **Explanation**: Capturing agent memory traces, corrections, and feedback provides the exact fine-tuning data needed to improve models over time.
